profiles.meeting_scenario: A coordination meeting between the editorial lead for an international update to the Conceptual Framework of Harmful Gambling and the knowledge-mobilization lead responsible for preparing the public-facing policy briefing package that will be released alongside the updated framework. The collaboration spans contributors in Canada, the UK, Australia, and New Zealand, and the team needs to align on shared artifacts, handoff timing, and what version of the framework materials will feed into downstream outputs. The agenda is to confirm which framework files are considered stable enough for handoff, what the 'final framework' package includes, how citations and examples should be carried into the policy brief, and who will update the shared diagram and glossary. The expected outcome is an apparently smooth agreement on the handoff plan for next week's cross-workstream deadline.

members.name: Dr. Maya Chen
members.role: Editorial Lead for the Framework Update
members.expertise: Public health synthesis, interdisciplinary research coordination, academic editing
members.background: Based in Toronto, Maya coordinates chapter leads and subject-matter reviewers for the updated harmful gambling framework and manages the master manuscript, contributor comments, and diagram revisions for the research consortium.
members.private_state: She wants to freeze the research-side materials quickly so the dispersed authors stop reopening settled language, but she is also worried that policy-facing simplifications could introduce wording the academic contributors have not approved.
hidden_assumptions: When people ask for the 'final framework,' they mean the near-final research package: the locked chapter text, current master diagram, and internal glossary notes, even if copyediting and permissions are still pending.
The 'latest diagram' means the master editable figure revised after the March reviewer call, not derivative formats exported for communications use.
If a team says they will 'carry over the examples,' they will preserve the jurisdictional balance and caveats already embedded in the academic draft rather than rewriting for audience accessibility.
Ownership of the glossary stays with editorial unless someone explicitly asks to alter definitions, so downstream teams can format it but should not substantively revise terms.

members.name: Elena Ruiz
members.expertise: Policy translation, stakeholder communications, cross-sector briefing materials
members.background: Based in Wellington, Elena prepares briefing decks, executive summaries, and partner-facing materials for public agencies and treatment organizations using outputs from international research collaborations.
members.private_state: She needs something stable enough to circulate to external design and translation vendors this week, and she wants the package to be self-contained so her team is not blocked by ongoing academic edits across time zones.
hidden_assumptions: When collaborators say a package is 'final,' they mean externally shareable and publication-safe, with permissions cleared and wording stable enough for design, translation, and stakeholder circulation.
The 'latest diagram' refers to the most presentation-ready version already resized and simplified for briefing materials, not the editable source figure with internal annotations.
To 'carry over the examples' means selecting a few representative examples and rewriting them in plainer language so policy readers can scan them quickly.

A glossary attached to a briefing package is a shared communications artifact, so the team preparing the briefing can streamline definitions for consistency without routing every wording tweak back to editorial.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the 'final framework' package
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to handing off the 'final framework' next week
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the research content has reached internal conceptual stability: chapter text, figure source files, and glossary notes are stable enough for downstream work, though copyediting, permissions checks, and a few wording refinements may still occur.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the package is safe for external circulation: no expected text changes, permissions resolved, and files packaged in the formats needed by design and translation vendors.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In cross-functional collaborations, 'final' is routinely used as a convenience label for the current approved stage; both are competent and optimistic, so each hears a familiar workflow milestone rather than a term needing definition.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss using the 'latest diagram' in the policy materials
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the editable master systems diagram updated after the March reviewer call, with all domains and relationship labels intact.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the communications-ready slide version exported after the April stakeholder webinar, which omits some secondary labels and uses simplified grouping for readability.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: There are multiple recent files with similar names derived from the same framework figure, and both participants reasonably assume the other is referring to the most recently useful version in their own workflow.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to 'carry over the examples'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that the brief should 'carry over the examples' from the framework
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this includes preserving the spread of examples across individual, family, community, and societal harms, along with the cautionary framing that examples are illustrative rather than exhaustive.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this means selecting only a small subset of the clearest examples and rewriting them into short policy-oriented callouts, dropping some framing text and level-specific balance if needed for space.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds like straightforward reuse rather than a decision about boundaries and omissions, so neither expects that 'carry over' hides a different sense of how much of the surrounding structure must travel with the examples.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that Elena's team can 'clean up the glossary' before the briefing goes out
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes M2's team will do formatting cleanup, style harmonization, and flag any substantive wording issues back to editorial for approval.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes her team can directly tighten and simplify the definitions themselves as part of preparing a policy-facing glossary, then circulate the finished version with the briefing package.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both see glossary work as secondary support material rather than a core intellectual decision, so the phrase 'clean up' feels operational and too minor to unpack despite implying different approval paths.

turns.inner_thought: I need to lock the research package enough that the chapter leads stop reopening settled wording. For me, the final framework is the near-final research set: stable chapter text, the current master figure, and glossary notes, even if copyediting, permissions, and a few minor refinements are still in flight. I mainly want to confirm Elena can work from that without inviting substantive rewording back into the manuscript.

I need something externally shareable and self-contained this week, or at least early next week, because I can't keep vendors waiting while authors in different time zones keep tweaking language.

turns.inner_thought: I want the examples to stay anchored in the framework's balance across individual, family, community, and societal harms, with the existing jurisdictional spread and caveats preserved. turns.inner_thought: The glossary should travel with the package, but editorial still owns the definitions. turns.inner_thought: Good, that gives us permission to streamline the glossary directly so the language matches the executive summary, slides, and partner brief. If it's part of the briefing package, it needs to read as a shared communications tool, not as editorial notes.
turns.utterance: Absolutely. We'll streamline the glossary language so the terminology is consistent across the executive summary, slides, and the partner brief.
